basis: New mission, no workbook source. Researched via WebSearch (Sep 2026). Key facts: Taiwan's average farmer age ~64 (official avg rose 53.4 in 2005 to 58.4 by 2020, DGBAS); agricultural workforce fell from ~1.55M (1978) to ~530,000 (2022), an ~66% drop, 80%+ now middle-aged/elderly (農傳媒, DGBAS census); YesHealth Group / 源鮮智慧農場 R&D team 2008, founded 2013, Taoyuan hydroponic plant factory, exported whole-farm tech to Shenzhen (2018), Denmark (2019), reached Vatican, combined daily output 4,400+ kg, WEF Technology Pioneer (company site, business press); NYCU 5G smart farm — real-time AI/5G soil sensors, year-round white strawberries, turmeric curcumin up 3-4x; Tainan City + 經緯航太科技 AI photo-based disease ID across 10 crop types; NTU Bio-Industrial Mechatronics orchid disease-recognition robot; Academia Sinica Agricultural Biotechnology Research Center (ABRC) — stress-tolerance (drought/disease/salinity) crop gene research, described only in general terms, no specific gene/variety invented; World Vegetable Center (WorldVeg), Tainan, founded 1971 as Asian Vegetable Research and Development Center (AVRDC) by Taiwan/US/Japan/Korea/Thailand/Philippines/South Vietnam + ADB, renamed 2008; grouper (石斑魚) aquaculture #1 world production value/#2 volume (2008 FAO), 30+ yrs breeding history, AIoT ponds monitor O2/temp/pH, Fisheries Agency's first onshore leopard coral grouper (東星斑) farming; plant-factory lighting ~50% setup cost, electricity ~1/3 running cost (up to 27% per Japanese estimate), un-subsidised indoor produce often costs more than field-grown, sector fragmented; Taiwan bans domestic GMO cultivation but allows labelled GMO feed/grain imports; grouper-farming know-how leaked to China competitors, Taiwan grouper export value fell ~NT$2.9-3 billion (TVBS, 台灣光華雜誌). "ASIAGA" named in the task brief could not be verified as a distinct real entity; the closest verified real institute matching that description is the World Vegetable Center (WorldVeg/AVRDC), Tainan — used instead. Level is carried by syntax and lexical load per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md, not by word count.

slides.1: Envision lettuce grown entirely inside a windowless warehouse, lit only by artificial LED panels instead of natural daylight through the glass. Does an arrangement like that still genuinely qualify as farming?
slides.2: SDG 2 explicitly calls for farming systems tough enough to survive real shocks and keep going long-term, which raises today's central question rather directly. Can technology genuinely replace the farmers Taiwan keeps losing?
slides.3: Taiwan's average farmer has now reached approximately 64 years of age, a figure that keeps climbing steadily with each passing year. This represents a labour crisis first, an agricultural one second.
slides.4: Taiwan's farming workforce has contracted sharply since 1978, declining from about 1.55 million workers to a mere 530,000 by 2022. The remaining workforce is dominated now by middle-aged and considerably older workers.
slides.5: Farm work remains physically demanding and financially unrewarding compared with city jobs, so younger generations rarely choose to inherit it willingly. Land consequently sits fallow, or gets leased to someone else.
slides.6: This raises an uncomfortable question worth sitting with carefully. Absent fresh recruits or genuinely transformative methods, who exactly will be cultivating our food, or harvesting our fish, two decades from now?
slides.7: Having exported its entire hydroponic farming system abroad, YesHealth now operates facilities reaching Shenzhen, Denmark and even the Vatican from its Taoyuan base. Genuine achievements have clearly already emerged in this space.
slides.8: Smart sensors are quietly transforming farm methods as well, in almost every region now. A university-built 5G farm grows strawberries outside their normal season, while boosting turmeric's natural health value considerably.
slides.9: Aquaculture has changed a great deal too, across the whole industry. Taiwan has long dominated grouper breeding globally, and sensors that monitor water quality have recently enabled onshore farming of an entirely new species.
slides.10: Rather than depending solely on a farmer's trained eye, a photo-based application developed in Tainan can now identify disease on its own. It covers ten distinct crops, catching problems before real damage spreads further.
slides.11: Researchers based in Tainan have also been quietly breeding hardier vegetable varieties since 1971. This work still continues feeding populations both domestically and considerably further afield across the entire globe.
slides.12: This is still not free of real limits, though. Taiwan still prohibits cultivating genetically modified crops domestically, although it freely and entirely imports modified grain for direct use as animal feed.
slides.13: Every LED fixture draws substantial electricity continuously, and that expense accumulates rather rapidly over time for every grower. Lighting alone can constitute roughly half of an indoor farm's total infrastructure investment.
slides.14: Should government subsidies never arrive, that steep power bill will keep growing regardless. Indoor-grown vegetables often cost more than the same vegetable grown in an open field, undercutting their own market appeal.
slides.15: Precisely the same dilemma afflicts aquaculture in a remarkably similar way. Taiwan's hard-won grouper expertise has leaked to rival operations nearby, and export revenue has since fallen by roughly three billion dollars.
slides.16: Inventing the technology was clearly never the hardest part of this challenge. Making it affordable, legal and protected from copying remains what Taiwan actually confronts most directly and clearly today.
slides.17: In summary, Taiwan has already deployed working farm technology, not merely laboratory prototypes or small pilot trials somewhere else. Genetics, LED systems and smart sensors now operate together in practice.
slides.18: Bridging this gap demands genuine expertise in engineering, biology and data science operating in concert, rather than good fortune alone. Several people occupying this very room could plausibly supply exactly that combination.
slides.19: This raises a question genuinely worth pursuing further, right now. What might a cheaper LED, a faster sensor, or a better-protected idea accomplish for a farmer without any successor whatsoever?
slides.20: This unusual growing space could plausibly represent farming's actual future, not merely a curiosity. Let's therefore shape that shift carefully, before the last farmer eventually departs without any successor at all.
